issues.title: Meta: 4.0 Release Ideas
issues.body:
Starting to get back into the issues a bit here. Opening this as a meta issue tracking the potential breaking changes we might want to include in a 4.0 release. Will add to this as I see new things

### Breaking
- [ ] Drop official support for [EOL Node versions](https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases) - definitely drop 16.x, 18.x, 20 is in maintenance mode, depending on when we release 4.0 we may be good to drop it. Also include newer versions of Node in the testing matrix. Note: we won't officially set an `engines`, we just won't test on older versions and make no guarantees of support
- [ ] Drop `esm` module from the CLI client - this is unnecessary in newer versions of Node. We just need to add a good amount of test and docs for the "correct way" to interop with `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.mts`, etc.
- [ ] Potentially setting `min: 0` for default [connection pool config](https://github.com/knex/knex/issues/3447#issuecomment-4126378671)
- [ ] A way to have flagged schema builder improvements applied in a way that they don't affect existing migrations. Will open an issue at some point to explain what I mean here
- [ ] Get rid of the [confusing message](https://github.com/knex/knex/pull/5681) "the pool is probably full" message in the `KnexTimeoutError` 
- [ ] Explicit connection lifecycle context & management, reworking to allow custom lifecycle behavior in acquisition & disposal management

### Features 

Note: these could be 3.x releases, but should definitely be done before 4.0

- [ ] Stop mutating [the db connection](https://github.com/knex/knex/pull/6346)
- [ ] External [Pooling Interop](https://github.com/knex/knex/issues/2665) (probably requires the above issue to do cleanly)
- [ ] Maybe a dedicated [TracingChannel](https://github.com/knex/knex/issues/6394)?
- [ ] Retry-ability on query execution errors

### Bugfixes

- [ ] MySQL Enum value escaping #4481
- [ ] `jsonSet` inconsistencies #5165

### Other

- [ ] Maybe some forms of modernization? Cleanup Lodash, etc. Don't want to try to promise too much just yet

issues.title: Handling of query read timeout in PG transaction BEGIN is not consistent
issues.body:
# Environment

Knex version: 0.95.10
Database + version: postgres, client pg@8.7.1, server PostgreSQL version 10
OS: node:12.22.3-alpine3.12

# Bug
I have been playing around with `query_timeout` recently and spotted that timeout during transaction BEGIN behaves differently for `.transaction()` and `.transaction(handlerFunc)`
To make it easily reproducible I have modified my `node_modules/pg/lib/client.js` code in method `query` adding this code before `if (readTimeout) {` condition:
```
  if (query.text.includes('BEGIN')) {
    console.log('#### Setting 1 msec timeout for BEGIN')
    readTimeout = 1
  }
```

My simple transaction code samples are:
Version 1:
```
let trx
try {
  trx = await db_connection.transaction()
  await trx.raw('SELECT col FROM tbl')
  await trx.commit()
} catch (exception) {
  if (trx) await trx.rollback()
}
```

Version 2:
```
const selectFunc = async (trx) => {
  await trx.raw('SELECT col FROM tbl')
}
await db_connection.transaction(selectFunc)
```

Version 1 returns a valid trx object, however `trx.raw` call on it throws an Error
```
{
	"name": "Error",
	"message": "Transaction query already complete, run with DEBUG=knex:tx for more info",
	"stack": "Error: Transaction query already complete, run with DEBUG=knex:tx for more info
				at completedError (/src/node_modules/knex/lib/execution/transaction.js:396:9)
				at /src/node_modules/knex/lib/execution/transaction.js:362:24
				at new Promise (<anonymous>)
				at Client_PG.trxClient.query (/src/node_modules/knex/lib/execution/transaction.js:358:12)
				at Runner.query (/src/node_modules/knex/lib/execution/runner.js:130:36)
				at ensureConnectionCallback (/src/node_modules/knex/lib/execution/internal/ensure-connection-callback.js:13:17)
				at Runner.ensureConnection (/src/node_modules/knex/lib/execution/runner.js:272:20)
				at processTicksAndRejections (internal/process/task_queues.js:97:5)
				at async Runner.run (/src/node_modules/knex/lib/execution/runner.js:30:19)
				at async Object.exports.getData (/src/models/postgreSQL/myTable.js:42:22)"
}
```
I have also checked that `trx.isCompleted()` returns `true` in this case

Version 2 throws an Error, but different:
```
{
	"name": "Error",
	"message": "BEGIN; - Query read timeout",
	"stack": "Error: BEGIN; - Query read timeout    
				at Timeout._onTimeout (/src/node_modules/pg/lib/client.js:533:21)
				at listOnTimeout (internal/timers.js:554:17)
				at processTimers (internal/timers.js:497:7)"
}
```

From my perspective the 2nd version behaves more accurate to me. The 1st one hides query timeout and instead returns a completed transaction object.

Is it a bug or feature?
issues.author: miszczu-drako

comments.body: This issue is being tracked as part of #6241 (Connection and Pooling Meta-Issue). Timeout handling is closely related to connection and pool management.
comments.author: mercmobily

comments.body:
Thank you for this detailed bug report. You've identified an important inconsistency in how Knex handles query timeouts during transaction BEGIN between the two transaction API styles.

The issue is that when a timeout occurs during the `BEGIN` statement of a transaction, the two transaction APIs behave very differently:

**Version 1: `await knex.transaction()` (manual transaction)**
- Returns a transaction object even though BEGIN timed out
- The transaction is silently marked as completed due to the timeout
- Subsequent queries on this transaction object throw "Transaction query already complete"
- The real timeout error is hidden from the user
- This is problematic because the user doesn't know why the transaction appears completed

**Version 2: `await knex.transaction(handlerFunc)` (callback transaction)**
- Throws the actual timeout error: "BEGIN; - Query read timeout"
- The user immediately knows what went wrong
- This is the correct behaviour

The first version is clearly buggy - it should throw the timeout error just like the second version does, rather than silently marking the transaction as completed and returning a seemingly valid transaction object that will fail on any subsequent operation.

This inconsistency makes error handling unpredictable depending on which transaction API you use. Users expect both APIs to behave the same way, especially for error conditions.

This issue has been added to our Connection and Pooling META issue #6241, where we are tracking all connection lifecycle and pool management problems. Timeout handling during transaction operations is a connection management concern because:

- Transaction BEGIN failures should properly release the connection back to the pool
- Error propagation needs to be consistent across both transaction APIs
- Timeout errors during BEGIN indicate connection or database issues that users need to be aware of

The correct behaviour should be:
1. Both transaction APIs should throw the timeout error when BEGIN times out
2. The connection should be properly cleaned up and returned to the pool
3. No transaction object should be returned if BEGIN failed

This issue will remain open and tracked under META #6241.

Related issues:
- #6241 - Connection and Pooling META issue
- #5434 - Timeout not preserved in clone()
- #4630 - Query timeouts after ~16 minutes
- #4423 - Migration statement timeout errors
comments.author: mercmobily

comments.body:
I looked into the cause of this on knex 3.3.0 (`master` has the same code). It isn't specific to timeouts. On the tested PostgreSQL path, the no-handler form resolves even when a single `BEGIN` or `SAVEPOINT` statement fails:

```js
const trx = await knex.transaction()
await trx.raw('select 1/0').catch(() => {}) // PostgreSQL has now aborted the transaction
const nested = await trx.transaction()       // SAVEPOINT fails with 25P02, yet this resolves
await nested.raw('select 1')                 // "Transaction query already complete"
```

**Cause.**

1. `Transaction.query()` catches the failure of the `BEGIN` or `SAVEPOINT` statement, records it on `executionPromise`, and resolves.
2. `_onAcquire()` then builds the transactor and calls the container regardless.
3. Without a handler, the container is the outer promise's `resolve`. Two settlements compete for that promise:
   - `resolve(transactor)`;
   - the rejection, which travels from `executionPromise` through `acquireConnection()` and `_promise` to `.catch(reject)`.
4. On PostgreSQL, `resolve` gets there first.

**It is a promise-settlement race, not a difference between databases:**

- **MySQL with an isolation level.** knex sends `SET TRANSACTION ...` and then `BEGIN`. When the first statement fails, the second call fails inside knex. The extra promise hops let the rejection win, so MySQL rejects.
- **Swapping the statement counts swaps the results.** A single failing `BEGIN` on MySQL (stubbed) resolves, exactly like PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL forced onto that two-statement begin (patched) rejects.
- **Counting hops predicts the flip.** Adding three no-op `.then()` hops to `Transaction_PG#begin()` turns the PostgreSQL result into a rejection, which is the count the hops predict.

**The handler form also misbehaves** (case 3 in the reproduction below). Its promise does reject with the real error, but only after the handler has run without a transaction. Application-side effects performed by the handler before its first database query can therefore occur even though transaction initialization failed.

**A possible correction.** Let a failed `BEGIN`, `SET TRANSACTION` or `SAVEPOINT` reject instead of being swallowed. `_onAcquire()`'s existing `.catch()` would then reject `executionPromise`, and the container would never be called.

I tested a possible correction locally against these cases and ordinary transaction paths, by patching `Transaction#query` and `Transaction_MySQL2#query` on 3.3.0:

- the manual form rejected with the database error;
- the handler was not called;
- the nested case rejected with `25P02`;
- ordinary commits, nested release and rollback, the three isolation levels, `transactionProvider`, and the ordering of sibling transactions behaved as before.

`Transaction_MySQL`, `Transaction_MySQL2` and `Transaction_MariaDB` override `query()`, so a change would need to go in each of them, or in a shared helper.

This was on PostgreSQL 18.6 with `pg` 8.23.1 and MySQL 8.0.44 with `mysql2` 3.24.6, on Node 24, and not inside knex's own test suite. If the approach is useful, I'm happy to prepare a PR.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction (PostgreSQL)</summary>

```js
// A failed BEGIN or SAVEPOINT does not reject transaction() without a handler; the handler form still runs the handler.
//   DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/scratch node knex-failed-begin.mjs
import knexFactory from 'knex'

const db = knexFactory({ client: 'pg', connection: process.env.DATABASE_URL, pool: { min: 0, max: 2 } })
const settle = (p) => p.then(() => 'resolved', (e) => `rejected: ${e.message.split('\n')[0]}`)
async function report(label, promise) {
  console.log(`${label}:`, await settle(promise))
  const trx = await promise.catch(() => null)
  if (trx) {
    console.log('   executionPromise:', await settle(trx.executionPromise))
    console.log('   isCompleted():', trx.isCompleted(), '| first query:', await settle(trx.raw('select 1')))
  }
}

// 1. A nested transaction inside a transaction that PostgreSQL has aborted (any failed statement does that).
const outer = await db.transaction()
await outer.raw('select 1/0').catch(() => {})
await report('1. trx.transaction() in an aborted transaction', outer.transaction())
await outer.rollback()

// 2. A top-level BEGIN that the server rejects ('snapshot' is SQL Server only, so PostgreSQL rejects the BEGIN).
await report('2. knex.transaction({ isolationLevel })', db.transaction({ isolationLevel: 'snapshot' }))

// 3. The handler form with the same BEGIN.
let handlerRan = false
console.log('3. knex.transaction(handler, { isolationLevel }):', await settle(db.transaction(async () => { handlerRan = true }, { isolationLevel: 'snapshot' })), '| handler ran:', handlerRan)

await db.destroy()
```

Output (knex 3.3.0, `pg` 8.23.1, PostgreSQL 18.6):

```text
1. trx.transaction() in an aborted transaction: resolved
   executionPromise: rejected: SAVEPOINT trx3; - current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
   isCompleted(): true | first query: rejected: Transaction query already complete, run with DEBUG=knex:tx for more info
2. knex.transaction({ isolationLevel }): resolved
   executionPromise: rejected: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL snapshot; - syntax error at or near "snapshot"
   isCompleted(): true | first query: rejected: Transaction query already complete, run with DEBUG=knex:tx for more info
3. knex.transaction(handler, { isolationLevel }): rejected: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL snapshot; - syntax error at or near "snapshot" | handler ran: true
```

</details>

issues.title: v3.3.0 (oracledb): "DPI-1011: connection was not acquired from a session pool" on destroyRawConnection
issues.body:
Hi! We upgraded to 3.3.0 and stumbled upon the following,

The oracledb dialect destroys pooled connections with:
```
destroyRawConnection(connection) {
  return connection.release({ drop: true });
}
```
But connections in the default pool are standalone, created via oracledb.getConnection(). `drop: true` is only valid for native pool connections. 
So on a standalone connection using oracle's thick mode this happens:
```
DPI-1011: connection was not acquired from a session pool
```
Thus, leaving the connection open.

I think this was introduced by PR #6414. We reverted back to 3.2.10 and the problem is gone. Another solution would be to move to a native pool, but I reckon this doesn't address the issue.
issues.author: ICitate

issues.title: SQLite: a failed COMMIT leaves the connection inside the transaction, every later BEGIN fails
issues.body:
Written by Claude

# Environment

Knex version: 3.3.0
Database: SQLite, `better-sqlite3` 13 (in memory)

# Bug

When `COMMIT` fails on SQLite, e.g. because a deferred foreign key constraint
is violated, SQLite keeps the transaction open: "If the COMMIT fails ... the
transaction remains active" (https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html).
knex rejects the transaction, which is right, but doesn't send `ROLLBACK`.
SQLite runs on a single connection, so that connection stays inside the old
transaction, and every later transaction fails on `BEGIN` with
`cannot start a transaction within a transaction`, until the process restarts.

PostgreSQL ends the transaction when `COMMIT` fails, so this is SQLite-specific.
Related: #6141 (a failing explicit `commit()` resolves), which goes through the
same commit path.

# Reproduction

```js
const Knex = require('knex')
const knex = Knex({
  client: 'better-sqlite3',
  connection: { filename: ':memory:' },
  useNullAsDefault: true
})

await knex.raw('pragma foreign_keys = on')
await knex.schema.createTable('parent', t => { t.integer('id').primary() })
await knex.raw(
  'create table child (id integer primary key, parent_id integer ' +
  'references parent(id) deferrable initially deferred)'
)

// Violates the deferred constraint, so COMMIT fails:
await knex.transaction(async trx => {
  await trx('child').insert({ id: 1, parent_id: 999 })
}).catch(e => console.log('1st:', e.message))

// Any later transaction:
await knex.transaction(async trx => {
  await trx('parent').insert({ id: 1 })
}).catch(e => console.log('2nd:', e.message))
```

Output:

```
1st: COMMIT; - FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
2nd: BEGIN; - cannot start a transaction within a transaction
```

# Expected

After a failed `COMMIT` on SQLite, knex sends `ROLLBACK` (or otherwise ends the
transaction on the connection), so that later transactions work.

issues.title: PostgreSQL: `executionPromise` resolves when COMMIT is answered with ROLLBACK (aborted transaction)
issues.body:
# Environment

Knex version: 3.3.0 (`master` has the same code)
Database + version: PostgreSQL 18.6 with `pg` 8.23.1
OS: macOS (arm64), Node 24.14.1

# Bug

**1. Behaviour.** After any statement fails inside a PostgreSQL transaction, the transaction is aborted. A later `COMMIT` is not an error: PostgreSQL rolls the transaction back and replies with the command tag `ROLLBACK`.

| Signal | Current | Expected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL reply to `COMMIT` | `ROLLBACK` | `ROLLBACK` |
| `trx.commit()` | Resolves | May continue resolving |
| `trx.executionPromise` | Resolves | Rejects |

`commit()` resolving with that reply is the documented contract. `executionPromise` resolving is not. The transactions guide says `executionPromise` is "rejected if it gets rolled back by DB itself". #3847 recommends `executionPromise` as the way to learn the outcome. In this case it reports the opposite of what happened.

The usual trigger is an application that catches a constraint violation inside a transaction and carries on. None of its writes is committed. Code that follows #3847 and awaits `executionPromise` is told the transaction succeeded.

A lost connection during `COMMIT` already rejects `executionPromise`. This report is the case where the server answers, and the command tag is `ROLLBACK`.

**2. Error message.** There is none. `commit()` resolves, and `executionPromise` resolves.

**3. Reduced test code.** It needs an empty scratch database.

```js
// PostgreSQL answers COMMIT in an aborted transaction with ROLLBACK, and knex resolves executionPromise.
//   DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/scratch node knex-commit-rollback.mjs
import knexFactory from 'knex'

const db = knexFactory({ client: 'pg', connection: process.env.DATABASE_URL, pool: { min: 0, max: 1 } })
const outcome = (trx) => trx.executionPromise.then(() => 'resolved', (e) => `rejected (${e.message.split('\n')[0]})`)
await db.raw('drop table if exists knex_outcome; create table knex_outcome (code text primary key)')
await db.raw(`insert into knex_outcome values ('dup')`)

const trx = await db.transaction()
await trx.raw(`insert into knex_outcome values ('case1')`)
await trx.raw(`insert into knex_outcome values ('dup')`).catch((e) => console.log('1. statement failed with', e.code))
const res = await trx.commit()
console.log('1. commit() resolved; server reply:', res?.response?.command, '| executionPromise:', await outcome(trx))
console.log('committed rows:', (await db.raw('select code from knex_outcome order by code')).rows.map((r) => r.code).join(', '))

await db.raw('drop table knex_outcome')
await db.destroy()
```

Recorded output of the same statements, from a run that also contained other cases:

```text
1. statement failed with 23505
1. commit() resolved; server reply: ROLLBACK | executionPromise: resolved
```

The row `case1` was not committed.

**Possible direction.** On PostgreSQL, recognize a `ROLLBACK` command tag returned in response to `COMMIT` as an unsuccessful transaction outcome. Reject `executionPromise` while preserving the existing `commit()` settlement contract.

The implementation could live in `Transaction_PG` or use a dialect-specific result check in the shared transaction machinery. The exact settlement path needs testing against both manual and handler transactions.

A server-reported `COMMIT` failure, such as a deferred constraint violation, already rejects `executionPromise`. The change should leave that alone.

**A regression test** can cover the duplicate-key case above, the same case in the handler form, and a deferred constraint failure at `COMMIT`.

**Behaviour change.** Code that awaits `executionPromise`, or uses the handler form, after a caught error inside the transaction will now see a rejection. That matches the documentation and the database. The detection is PostgreSQL-specific, which is why this is an issue rather than a patch.

**Related:**

- #3847: `commit()` should not throw, and the outcome is read from `executionPromise`.
- #3370: a serialization error at `COMMIT` is not thrown.
- #6141: deferred-constraint errors at `COMMIT` are not thrown.
- #5887: document the commit and rollback behaviour.
- #6546: a different defect. A `ROLLBACK` or `COMMIT` that never reaches the server leaves the transaction open on a pooled connection.
issues.author: KevinBlakeLopez

issues.title: Connection returned to the pool with an open transaction when ROLLBACK or COMMIT fails on the client (e.g. pg `query_timeout`)
issues.body:
# Environment Knex version: 3.3.0 (`master` has the same code) Database + version: PostgreSQL 18.6 with `pg` 8.23.1; also MySQL 8.0.44 with `mysql2` 3.24.6 (see below) OS: macOS (arm64), Node 24.14.1 # Bug **1. Behaviour.** When a transaction's `ROLLBACK` or `COMMIT` fails on the client without reaching the server, knex still releases the connection to the pool, with the transaction open on it. The next transaction on that connection starts nothing (PostgreSQL only warns "there is already a transaction in progress"), and its `COMMIT` commits the earlier transaction's writes as well. A documented `pg` option is enough to cause this, without fault injection. With `query_timeout`, a statement that runs longer fails on the client but keeps running on the server. The transaction's `ROLLBACK` or `COMMIT` then waits in `pg`'s queue behind that statement, and when its own timer fires, `pg` removes it from the queue without sending it. - **The handler throws, so knex rolls back.** The transaction rejects, but the next transaction on that connection commits its writes. - **The handler catches the timeout and returns, so knex commits.** - The transaction rejects with `COMMIT; - Query read timeout`, and at that point nothing is committed. - The next transaction on that connection then commits those writes. If it rolls back instead, they are lost. - Either way, the outcome is decided by unrelated work. I'd expect knex never to hand a connection to other work while its transaction state is uncertain. - **After a top-level `ROLLBACK` or `COMMIT` fails,** the connection would go back to the pool only if the session is known to be outside a transaction. - **Otherwise knex would destroy it,** and PostgreSQL would roll back whatever was still open. This is only about reusing the connection. The transaction should still reject, as it does now. An idle session says nothing about whether the transaction committed. **2. Error message.** - `ROLLBACK - Query read timeout`, which replaces the statement's own error. - `COMMIT; - Query read timeout`. Nothing indicates that the connection went back to the pool. **3. Reduced test code.** It needs an empty scratch database.
knex-open-transaction-reuse.mjs ```js // A transaction whose ROLLBACK or COMMIT was never sent goes back to knex's pool with the transaction still open. // DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/scratch node knex-open-transaction-reuse.mjs // // node-postgres's query_timeout fails a query on the client after the given time. The timed-out statement keeps // running on the server, and a query that is still waiting in the client's queue when its own timer fires is // removed from the queue without being sent. import knexFactory from 'knex' const url = process.env.DATABASE_URL const db = knexFactory({ client: 'pg', connection: { connectionString: url, query_timeout: 1000 }, pool: { min: 0, max: 2 } }) const observer = knexFactory({ client: 'pg', connection: url, pool: { min: 0, max: 1 } }) // reads committed rows only const committed = async () => (await observer.raw('select code from knex_reuse order by code')).rows.map((r) => r.code).join(', ') const backend = async (trx) => (await trx.raw('select pg_backend_pid() as pid')).rows[0].pid const pause = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)) await observer.raw('drop table if exists knex_reuse; create table knex_reuse (code text primary key)') async function nextUnitOfWork(code) { await pause(1500) // let the 3 s statement finish on the server first, so these statements are not queued behind it return db.transaction(async (trx) => { const pid = await backend(trx) await trx.raw('insert into knex_reuse values (?)', [code]) return pid }) } // 1. A statement outlives query_timeout and the handler throws, so knex rolls back. let pid await db.transaction(async (trx) => { pid = await backend(trx) await trx.raw(`insert into knex_reuse values ('rolled-back')`) await trx.raw('select pg_sleep(3)') }).catch((e) => console.log('1. transaction rejected:', e.message)) console.log(`1. next transaction ran on backend ${await nextUnitOfWork('next-1')} (first: ${pid}); committed: ${await committed()}`) // 2. The handler catches the timed-out statement and returns, so knex commits. await observer.raw('truncate knex_reuse') await db.transaction(async (trx) => { pid = await backend(trx) await trx.raw(`insert into knex_reuse values ('reported-as-failed')`) await trx.raw('select pg_sleep(3)').catch(() => {}) }).catch(async (e) => console.log('2. transaction rejected:', e.message, `| committed: ${(await committed()) || '(none)'}`)) console.log(`2. next transaction ran on backend ${await nextUnitOfWork('next-2')} (first: ${pid}); committed: ${await committed()}`) await observer.raw('drop table knex_reuse') await Promise.all([db.destroy(), observer.destroy()]) ```
Output. The PostgreSQL log shows that neither the `ROLLBACK` nor the `COMMIT` was sent: ```text 1. transaction rejected: ROLLBACK - Query read timeout 1. next transaction ran on backend 152 (first: 152); committed: next-1, rolled-back 2. transaction rejected: COMMIT; - Query read timeout | committed: (none) 2. next transaction ran on backend 152 (first: 152); committed: next-2, reported-as-failed ```
PostgreSQL log (log_statement = all) ```text LOG: statement: BEGIN; LOG: statement: insert into knex_reuse values ('rolled-back') LOG: statement: select pg_sleep(3) LOG: statement: BEGIN; WARNING: there is already a transaction in progress LOG: execute : insert into knex_reuse values ($1) DETAIL: Parameters: $1 = 'next-1' LOG: statement: COMMIT; LOG: statement: BEGIN; LOG: statement: insert into knex_reuse values ('reported-as-failed') LOG: statement: select pg_sleep(3) LOG: statement: BEGIN; WARNING: there is already a transaction in progress LOG: execute : insert into knex_reuse values ($1) DETAIL: Parameters: $1 = 'next-2' LOG: statement: COMMIT; ```
**Where it happens.** - At release, a read of `client.getTransactionStatus()` was still `'T'`. knex does not call that method. - `Transaction.query()` records the failed statement on `executionPromise`. - `acquireConnection()`'s `finally` then releases the connection unconditionally. - The failed `ROLLBACK` or `COMMIT` does not mark the connection `__knex__disposed`. knex's default PostgreSQL `validate` then accepts it. That check looks at the disposed flag, the connection lifetime, a config refresh, and a user hook, then `validateConnection()`, which returns true. It does not look at transaction status. A `connectionPool` does not use this `validate`. - tarn hands out the most recently released connection first, so this does not need `max: 1`. **Further effects** (same setup): - **A query outside a transaction** on that connection resolves, but it only joins the leftover transaction. No other session sees it, and it is lost when the connection closes. - **A poisoned connection.** If any statement fails while the leftover transaction is open, PostgreSQL aborts it. From then on every transaction and every query on that connection fails with `25P02` (`current transaction is aborted`): 20 of 20 of each in our run. knex keeps handing the connection out. - **Other setups.** The same release happens with `connectionPool: new pg.Pool()`, and on MySQL. On MySQL the next `BEGIN` implicitly commits the leftover transaction. If that next transaction then rolls back, the earlier writes stay committed. These two were checked with a `ROLLBACK` made to fail on the client by a stub. **Suggested direction.** **The rule.** After a top-level `ROLLBACK` or `COMMIT` fails, release the connection only if the driver reports that the session is idle. Otherwise mark it `__knex__disposed`. - **knex already uses that flag** to discard connections it can't trust: - a query that timed out without being cancelled (`runner.js`); - SQLite's `_logAndDispose`; - connection errors. - **Both pool types honour it:** the pool's `validate`, and the pg `connectionPool` adapter (`release(true)`). - **Success paths are unchanged.** **The signal.** For PostgreSQL, the connection knex holds is the `pg` client itself. `pg` 8.21+ provides `client.getTransactionStatus()`. - **What it returns:** the transaction-status byte of the last ReadyForQuery message the server sent: `'I'` idle, `'T'` in a transaction, `'E'` in a failed transaction. - **Reading it sends nothing to the server,** so it cannot change the session or hide the original error. - **It can lag by one message.** Right after an error, the server's ReadyForQuery may not have been processed yet. - In the tested failure sequences, stale values caused conservative disposal: a connection was discarded even though its transaction had already ended. - A production implementation should verify that an idle status cannot be stale in the unsafe direction at the point of release. **When the state can't be established,** destroy the connection. That covers `pg` older than 8.21, and drivers without such a signal. For example, `mysql2` reports `SERVER_STATUS_IN_TRANS` on each result, but has no accessor for the connection's current state. **Alternatives we measured against:** - **Destroying unconditionally.** Server-reported `COMMIT` failures end the transaction and leave a healthy connection, for example a deferred constraint or `40001`. Destroying those too costs a reconnect after each one: 20 for 20 in our run. - **Sending a statement to find out**, for example a `ROLLBACK` on acquire. It costs a round trip each time, and it acts on a session whose state is unknown. **The MySQL family needs the change separately.** `Transaction_MySQL`, `Transaction_MySQL2` and `Transaction_MariaDB` override `query()`, so a change only in the base class does not reach them. We checked this with `mysql2`.
Simulated options (PostgreSQL) | Change | `ROLLBACK` failing (stubbed) | `ROLLBACK` dropped | `COMMIT` dropped | 20 deferred-FK failures at `COMMIT` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | none (3.3.0) | reused; row committed | reused; row committed | reused; row committed | 1 connection | | dispose on a failed `ROLLBACK` | new connection; row absent | new; absent | **reused; row committed** | 1 | | dispose on a failed `ROLLBACK` or `COMMIT` | new; absent | new; absent | new; absent | **20 connections** | | the same, unless `getTransactionStatus() === 'I'` (the rule above) | new; absent | new; absent | new; absent | 1 to 2 across two runs; one extra reconnect when the status was stale | | pool `validate`: `getTransactionStatus() === 'I'` | new; absent | new; absent | new; absent | 1 |
**A regression test** can use `pool: { max: 1 }` and make one `ROLLBACK` fail on the client with a stub, which is deterministic. It then asserts that the next transaction reports a different `pg_backend_pid()`, and that the first transaction's row is absent. I'm happy to work on a PR if this approach aligns with the maintainers' expectations. **Partial mitigation**, with knex's own pool and `pg` 8.21+: `pool: { validate: (conn) => conn.getTransactionStatus() === 'I' }`. This checks the last observed transaction status, not an independently verified current server state, and does not replace transaction cleanup. It is not available with `connectionPool`. **Related:** - #3847: the outcome is read from `executionPromise`; nothing here changes that. - #1296: rollback errors on a dead connection are ignored on purpose. - #4709: the same `query_timeout`, on `BEGIN`. - #6241: the connection and pool meta issue. - #6545: SQLite keeps a transaction open after a failed `COMMIT`.

issues.title: Fixing Knex's GROUP BY Parameter Duplication Issue
issues.body:
While #2806 is a documentation issue, I do believe we should try and solve the problem properly.

Thing is, when using the same Raw expression in both SELECT and GROUP BY clauses, Knex creates separate parameter bindings, causing PostgreSQL to treat them as different expressions:

```javascript
const field = knex.raw('??#>>?', ['attributes', ['job']]);
knex('users').select(field).groupBy(field);

// Generates:
// SELECT "attributes"#>>$1 FROM users GROUP BY "attributes"#>>$2
// Parameters: [['job'], ['job']]
```

PostgreSQL requires exact expression matching between SELECT and GROUP BY, so it throws: `column must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function`.

What can be done?

## Possible Solutions

### 1. Parameter Deduplication System (Most Elegant)

Implement a system that tracks and reuses parameter positions for identical values:

```javascript
class ParameterManager {
  constructor() {
    this.params = [];
    this.paramMap = new Map(); // Map of value -> position
  }
  
  addParameter(value) {
    const key = JSON.stringify(value); // or a hash
    if (this.paramMap.has(key)) {
      return this.paramMap.get(key); // Return existing position
    }
    this.params.push(value);
    const position = this.params.length;
    this.paramMap.set(key, position);
    return position;
  }
}
```

**Result:** `SELECT "attributes"#>>$1 FROM users GROUP BY "attributes"#>>$1`

**Pros:**
- Maintains security with parameterized queries
- Fixes the issue transparently
- Reduces redundant parameters (performance benefit)

**Cons:**
- Breaking change if anyone relies on parameter order <--- This is the biggest problem
- Complex handling for objects/arrays
- Needs careful implementation to avoid hash collisions

### 2. Raw Instance Tracking (Pragmatic)

Track when the same Raw instance is used multiple times and compile it only once:

```javascript
class QueryCompiler {
  constructor() {
    this.compiledRaws = new WeakMap();
  }
  
  compileRaw(rawInstance) {
    if (this.compiledRaws.has(rawInstance)) {
      return this.compiledRaws.get(rawInstance);
    }
    const compiled = /* compile the raw */;
    this.compiledRaws.set(rawInstance, compiled);
    return compiled;
  }
}
```

**Pros:**
- Only affects identical Raw instances
- Backwards compatible
- Simpler to implement

**Cons:**
- Only works if users reuse the same instance
- Doesn't help if users create separate but identical Raw expressions
- Limited scope of fix

### 3. Expression Registry with Automatic Aliases (Most Robust)

Automatically generate and track aliases for complex expressions:

```javascript
// Knex internally generates:
// SELECT: "attributes"#>>$1 AS __expr_hash_abc123
// GROUP BY: __expr_hash_abc123
```

**Pros:**
- Always works regardless of how expressions are created
- No parameter duplication issues
- PostgreSQL handles it correctly

**Cons:**
- Changes output column names (unless carefully managed)
- More complex SQL generation
- May affect existing code expecting specific column names

### 4. Dialect-Specific GROUP BY Optimization (PostgreSQL-specific)

For PostgreSQL, detect when GROUP BY contains expressions from SELECT and use positional references or aliases:

```javascript
// Option A: Positional
SELECT "attributes"#>>$1 AS job FROM users GROUP BY 1

// Option B: Alias reference  
SELECT "attributes"#>>$1 AS job FROM users GROUP BY job
```

**Pros:**
- Solves the PostgreSQL issue directly
- Clean SQL output
- No parameter duplication

**Cons:**
- PostgreSQL-specific solution
- Positional GROUP BY can be fragile with query modifications
- Requires detecting which expressions in GROUP BY match SELECT

### 5. New API Methods (Explicit Control)

Add new methods that give users explicit control over expression reuse:

```javascript
// Method 1: groupByAlias - reference a column alias
knex('users')
  .select(knex.raw('??#>>?', ['attributes', ['job']]).as('job'))
  .groupByAlias('job')  // New method!

// Method 2: expression objects that track their usage
const expr = knex.expression('??#>>?', ['attributes', ['job']]);
knex('users')
  .select(expr.as('job'))
  .groupBy(expr)  // Knex knows to reuse the same parameter positions

// Method 3: explicit parameter sharing
knex('users')
  .select(knex.raw('??#>>?', ['attributes', ['job']]).as('job'))
  .groupBy(knex.raw.ref('job'))  // Reference the alias
```

**Pros:**
- Backwards compatible (new opt-in features)
- Explicit and predictable
- Can ship in a minor version
- Gives users immediate workarounds

**Cons:**
- Requires users to change their code
- Doesn't fix existing code automatically
- Multiple ways to do the same thing (API complexity)

We could combine #1 and #5

### Short Term (Immediate Relief)

Implement **Solution #5 (New API Methods)** first:
- Ship in next minor version (e.g., 3.2.0)
- Provides immediate workarounds for affected users
- Fully backwards compatible
- Clear migration path

Example implementation:
```javascript
// New methods available immediately
knex('users')
  .select(knex.raw('??#>>?', ['attributes', ['job']]).as('job_field'))
  .groupByAlias('job_field')  // New!

// Or with expression tracking
const jobExpr = knex.expression('??#>>?', ['attributes', ['job']]);
knex('users')
  .select(jobExpr.as('job'))
  .groupBy(jobExpr)  // Reuses same parameters
```

### Long Term (Proper Fix)

Implement **Solution #1 (Parameter Deduplication)** with careful rollout:
1. **Version 3.3.0:** Add behind feature flag
   ```javascript
   knex({ 
     deduplicateParameters: true  // Opt-in
   })
   ```

2. **Version 3.4.0:** Enable by default with opt-out
   ```javascript
   knex({ 
     deduplicateParameters: false  // Opt-out for compatibility
   })
   ```

3. **Version 4.0.0:** Remove flag, always deduplicate

## Why This Combination?

1. **Immediate Relief:** Users suffering from this issue get solutions now
2. **Proper Fix:** The underlying problem gets solved correctly
3. **Migration Path:** Clear upgrade path with feature flags
4. **Backwards Compatibility:** No breaking changes until major version
5. **Best Practices:** Maintains parameterized queries throughout

## Implementation Priority

1. **First:** Add `groupByAlias()` method (easiest, most useful)
2. **Second:** Add `knex.expression()` for trackable expressions
3. **Third:** Implement parameter deduplication behind flag
4. **Finally:** Make deduplication default in next major version

## Alternative for Users (Available Now)

Until these fixes are implemented, users can work around the issue:

```javascript
// Workaround: Use aliases
knex('users')
  .select(knex.raw('??#>>? as job_field', ['attributes', ['job']]))
  .groupBy('job_field')

// This works because GROUP BY references the alias, not the expression
```

## Conclusion

The parameter duplication issue represents a fundamental tension between:
- PostgreSQL's strict expression matching requirements
- Security best practices (parameterized queries)
- Query builder architecture (independent clause compilation)

The recommended dual approach provides both immediate relief and a long-term solution, maintaining security while fixing the underlying architectural issue.

comments.body:
I don't know how and where you want to add the deduplication exactly but a quick note/warning. At Ambassify we had implemented parameter deduplication ourselves and ran into a problem for inserts on Postgres. What would happen is this:

Let's say you have a table `stuff` that has two columns:

- `foo`: `varchar(255)`
- `bar`: `text` 

When we would then (with our parameter deduplication enabled) use knex to insert a row:

```js
await knex('stuff').insert({ foo: 'test', bar: 'test' });
```

Our deduplication would kick in and the query would end up looking like:

`INSERT INTO stuff (foo, bar) VALUES ($1, $1)` with bindings `[ 'test' ]`

And cause Postgres to error out with:

> Inconsistent types deduced for parameter $1

We didn't find a good solution for it yet and resorted to toggling deduplication manually in the application code (using `queryContext`).
